title: EchoNext flags the pre-operative ECG of an 84-year-old woman with no heart symptoms; echocardiography shows severe aortic stenosis, and she undergoes valve replacement after surgery for a broken femur
summary: At Columbia, the EchoNext deep-learning model flagged an 84-year-old's pre-operative ECG; echocardiography then showed severe aortic stenosis, and she had a valve replacement after her surgery.
account: EchoNext is a deep-learning model for structural heart disease developed at Columbia. Its development paper (Poterucha et al., Nature, July 2025) reports training on more than 1 million electrocardiogram (ECG) and imaging records. It reports that 73% of patients flagged high-risk in prospective evaluation had newly diagnosed disease. Tat et al. (JACC: Case Reports, 4 March 2026) describe an 84-year-old woman with hypertension. She was admitted after a fall with a left femur fracture. Her ECG was analyzed by EchoNext. The score was 0.6094; the model's high-risk cutoff is 0.6. The score triggered an electronic health record (EHR) advisory. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 40% and severe aortic stenosis. The valve area was 0.6 cm2, peak velocity 3.9 m/s and mean gradient 34 mm Hg. Cardiology recommended cardiac anesthesia for the orthopedic operation. The patient then underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), on day 8. The authors call it the first report of an AI-ECG algorithm detecting undiagnosed severe aortic stenosis that led to TAVR. The case report comes from Columbia authors who include the model's developers Poterucha and Elias. Dr. Elias reports research support including from Edwards. The journal received the case report on 18 November 2025, so the events took place before then, during pilot testing of EchoNext at Columbia. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared EchoNext through a 510(k) on 8 June 2026, with Pathwai, Inc. as the applicant. In the sponsor's validation, the aortic stenosis output had a sensitivity of 54.9% and a positive predictive value of 11.8%. A NewYork-Presbyterian release of 23 June 2026 calls the clearance an approval. An independent team at Thomas Jefferson University reported in September 2026 that the smaller released EchoNext-Mini model kept most of its accuracy in another hospital's records. In 45,878 Boston patients, its composite area under the curve was 0.790, against 0.820 on the benchmark test set. The team did not test the deployed model or this case.

data.answer:
At Columbia/NewYork-Presbyterian, EchoNext flagged a pre-operative ECG (score 0.6094), triggering an EHR advisory; echo showed LVEF 40% and severe aortic stenosis; cardiac anesthesia, surgery, TAVR.

The echocardiogram and clinicians established the diagnosis and treatment. A case report cannot show that the alert prevented death or surgical complications, and no untreated comparison is available. The abstract does not establish long-term recovery or the net consequences of false-positive alerts.

display.answer: The patient's course comes only from the developers' case report. The Nature development paper, the FDA 510(k) summary and the NewYork-Presbyterian release also come from the makers. The Thomas Jefferson University team tested the smaller EchoNext-Mini model independently and did not examine this case.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: At Columbia, the EchoNext deep-learning model flagged an 84-year-old's pre-operative ECG; echocardiography then showed severe aortic stenosis, and she had a valve replacement after her surgery.
fields.account: EchoNext is a deep-learning model for structural heart disease developed at Columbia. Its development paper (Poterucha et al., Nature, July 2025) reports training on more than 1 million electrocardiogram (ECG) and imaging records. It reports that 73% of patients flagged high-risk in prospective evaluation had newly diagnosed disease. Tat et al. (JACC: Case Reports, 4 March 2026) describe an 84-year-old woman with hypertension. She was admitted after a fall with a left femur fracture. Her ECG was analyzed by EchoNext. The score was 0.6094; the model's high-risk cutoff is 0.6. The score triggered an electronic health record (EHR) advisory. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 40% and severe aortic stenosis. The valve area was 0.6 cm2, peak velocity 3.9 m/s and mean gradient 34 mm Hg. Cardiology recommended cardiac anesthesia for the orthopedic operation. The patient then underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), on day 8. The authors call it the first report of an AI-ECG algorithm detecting undiagnosed severe aortic stenosis that led to TAVR. The case report comes from Columbia authors who include the model's developers Poterucha and Elias. Dr. Elias reports research support including from Edwards. The journal received the case report on 18 November 2025, so the events took place before then, during pilot testing of EchoNext at Columbia. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared EchoNext through a 510(k) on 8 June 2026, with Pathwai, Inc. as the applicant. In the sponsor's validation, the aortic stenosis output had a sensitivity of 54.9% and a positive predictive value of 11.8%. A NewYork-Presbyterian release of 23 June 2026 calls the clearance an approval. An independent team at Thomas Jefferson University reported in September 2026 that the smaller released EchoNext-Mini model kept most of its accuracy in another hospital's records. In 45,878 Boston patients, its composite area under the curve was 0.790, against 0.820 on the benchmark test set. The team did not test the deployed model or this case.
